analysis.one_liner: Lets courts dismiss bad-faith corporate bankruptcies used to cap liability for mass injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 with support from two Democrats and one Republican, but has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since the day it was introduced with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets a bankruptcy maneuver sometimes called the 'Texas two-step,' in which a large company splits itself in two before filing Chapter 11, leaving the liabilities — often injury claims from a product like talc or asbestos — with one entity that then files for bankruptcy. The bankruptcy can cap or wipe out what injured people are paid, while the healthier affiliate is protected. The bill would let bankruptcy courts dismiss filings that are futile or in bad faith, presume bad faith when a company manufactured the venue or did a divisional merger within the prior four years, and allow injury lawsuits to proceed against non-bankrupt affiliates rather than freezing them under the automatic stay.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mass injury claims — the bill's 'protected claims' cover groups of 100 or more individuals harmed by a product, material, or substance — and ordinary creditors, who would no longer see claims buried in a bankruptcy engineered to cap them. Communities exposed to toxic products keep their day in court against the parent companies that profited.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a Chapter 11 filing that is objectively futile or filed in subjective bad faith a ground for dismissal or conversion of the case.
Creates a presumption of bad faith when the debtor manufactured the bankruptcy venue, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence with the burden on the debtor.

Creates a conclusive (irrebuttable) presumption of bad faith when, within the prior four years, the debtor was subject to a divisional merger or similar restructuring, transferred substantial assets to insiders or affiliates, or lacks a valid reorganizational purpose.

Carves mass-tort claims — those affecting 100 or more individuals from exposure to a product or substance, or claims against non-debtor owners, officers, or insurers tied to the debtor — out of the automatic stay, so lawsuits can proceed against healthy non-bankrupt affiliates.
Bars bankruptcy courts from issuing orders that override or nullify that stay exception, closing off the tactic of using bankruptcy injunctions to shield non-debtor affiliates from mass injury suits.
Applies to cases filed or pending on or after enactment, so it reaches bankruptcies already underway.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass injury liability and the restructuring advisers and private equity owners who use split-off bankruptcies. They would lose the ability to cap or channel liability through bankruptcy and would face full claims in ordinary courts.

drawbacks.text: The conclusive bad-faith presumption for any divisional merger within four years, with the debtor bearing the burden of proof, could push genuinely distressed companies that restructured in good faith into dismissal and liquidation, which would cost jobs and leave ordinary creditors worse off.

The bill applies retroactively to cases already pending, which could unwind business planning that was lawful when it happened and disrupt settlements already being negotiated, though it protects previously confirmed plans.

Some ordinary creditors actually recover more in an orderly bankruptcy than in piecemeal mass-tort litigation; the bill acknowledges this by directing courts to weigh whether a creditors' committee supports dismissal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims of engineered bankruptcies, the benefit is real and large: the bill strikes directly at the specific moves — manufactured venue, divisional mergers, insider asset transfers, and non-debtor injunctions — that have capped payouts in well-known mass-tort cases. The cost is that its presumptions are blunt, and the conclusive presumption for any recent divisional merger could catch legitimate restructurings in the net, with job losses and lower recoveries for ordinary creditors. A better-drafted version might use rebuttable presumptions; as written, the anti-abuse rules are strong but imprecise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 20, 2026, joined by Senator Josh Hawley and Senator Dick Durbin.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action — appears in the action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that use split-off bankruptcies to cap mass injury liability are better off, since the bill has not advanced and this Congress ends in January 2027. Restructuring advisers who sell the strategy also keep their playbook intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies capping liability via bankruptcy maneuvers

sides.party_line_note: Two Democrats and one Republican originally sponsored the bill, but with only two cosponsors and no votes ever taken, no bloc-level partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill makes the split-off bankruptcy playbook presumptively bad faith and lets injury claims proceed against non-bankrupt parents and affiliates, so these companies would face full liability in ordinary courts instead of capping it in bankruptcy. Their gain historically has come directly out of what injured people are paid.

industries.industry: Restructuring advisers and private equity owners
industries.note: The strategy of dividing a company before filing Chapter 11 to ring-fence tort liabilities is the bill's explicit target, framed as a divisional merger within four years of filing. Firms selling this service would lose a lucrative and legally powerful tool.
More claims against non-debtor affiliates would survive the automatic stay, expanding the pool of viable mass-tort cases. When victims win more, this industry wins alongside them.

analysis.trajectory: With only its three original sponsors, no cosponsors added since April, and no committee action for months, the bill is likely to die in the Senate Judiciary Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027; the realistic next step, if anything, is a future reintroduction in the next Congress.
